The first: he had a wife called Jarada, and between some of her relatives and a people there was a dispute; he judged between them with truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. He was punished because his inclination was not even toward both parties. Allah Most High revealed to him that a trial would befall him, and he did not know whether it would come to him from the heaven or from the earth. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: his wife Jarada was the dearest of the women to him, and she said to him one day: "My brother has a dispute with so-and-so, and I love that you judge in his favor." He said: "Yes," but did not do so, and he was tested because of what he had said. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: his wife Jarada had been taken by him as a captive in a raid, and she was a king's daughter who had embraced Islam, and she wept constantly by night and day in his presence. He asked her about her condition, and she said: "I remember my father and what I was in. If only you would command the devils to fashion his likeness in my house, so that I might console myself with it." [He did so], and whenever Sulayman went out, she and her maidservants prostrated to it for forty mornings. When Sulayman learned of this, he broke that image, punished the woman and her maidservants, then humbled himself before Allah Most High, seeking forgiveness for what had been in his house. So the devil was given power over his ring. [This is the saying of Wahb ibn Munabbih.] The fourth: he secluded himself from the people for three days, and Allah Most High revealed to him: "O Sulayman, you have secluded yourself from the people for three days and have not looked into the affairs of My servants, nor given justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer?" So the devil was given power over his ring. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. The fifth: he approached one of his wives during menstruation or otherwise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second view: that what is meant by the body cast upon his throne is that a son was born to him, and the devils gathered together, and some of them said to others: "If a son of his survives, it will not benefit you from the trial. (p-135) Our course is to kill his son or to cripple him." Sulayman learned of this, [so he commanded the clouds], which carried him away, and his son ran off into the clouds out of fear of the devils. Allah Most High rebuked him for his fear of the devils, and the child died, and he was cast upon his throne as a dead body. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The exegetes hold the first view. We will mention the story of his testing according to the view of the majority.

Indication of that:

The scholars differed about how the ring of Sulayman was lost, according to two views.

The first: he was sitting on the shore of the sea, and it fell from him into the sea. This was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: a devil took it, and regarding the manner of that there are four views.

The first: he entered the bathhouse one day and placed the ring beneath his bedding, and the devil came and took it and threw it into the sea, and the devil began saying: "I am the Prophet of Allah." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: Sulayman said to the devil: "How do you tempt people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will inform you." So he gave it to him, and he threw it into the sea, and Sulayman's kingdom departed, and the devil sat upon his throne. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: he entered the bathhouse, and placed his ring with his most trusted wife, (p-136) and the devil came to her in the form of Sulayman and took the ring from her. When Sulayman came out, he asked her for it, and she said: "I have already given it to you." Sulayman fled, and the devil came and sat upon his kingdom. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: he entered the bathhouse and gave his ring to the devil, and the devil threw it into the sea, so Sulayman's kingdom departed, and his likeness was cast upon the devil. This was said by Qatadah.

As for the story of the devil, most of the exegetes mention that when he took the ring he threw it into the sea, and his likeness was cast upon him, so he sat upon his throne and domineered over his realm.

And al-Suddi said: "He did not throw it into the sea until he fled from Solomon's place." Did [the wives of] Solomon get visited by him? On this there are two opinions. One: he was not able to have them, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: he would come to them during menstruation, and they rejected him, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib; the first is more correct. They said: he would issue unsound judgments and rule by what is not permissible, so the Children of Israel denounced him. Some of them said to others: "Either you have perished, or your kingdom has perished. Go to his wives and ask them." So they went, and the wives said: "By God, we have indeed rejected that." He remained in his state until the period of trial came to an end.

Regarding the manner of the Satan's distance from Solomon's place, there are four opinions.
One of them: Solomon found his ring and put it on, then came and seized the forelock of the Satan, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.
The second: when Solomon returned to his kingdom and the wind, the birds and the devils came to him, the Satan fled until he entered the sea, said by Mujahid.
The third: when forty days had passed, the Satan flew from his assembly, said by Wahb.
The fourth: when the Children of Israel denounced him, they came to him and surrounded him, then they unfolded the Torah and read, and he flew before them until he went to the sea, and the ring fell from him into the sea, and a fish swallowed it, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding how long the Satan remained, there are two opinions. One: forty days, said by most. The second: fourteen days, related by al-Tha'labi.

As for the story of Solomon, peace be upon him: when his ring was taken from him, his kingdom was lost, and he set off fleeing across the land. Mujahid said: he would ask for food and not be fed, so he would say, "If you knew me, you would give to me. I am Solomon," and they would drive him away, until a woman gave him a fish, and he found his ring in the belly of the fish. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Solomon set off until he reached the seashore, and he found fishermen who had caught a great deal of fish, some of which had begun to rot. He came to them asking for food. They said, "Go to those fish and take some from them." He said, "No, feed me from this." They refused him, so he said, "Feed me, for I am Solomon." A man among them leapt at him and struck him with a stick out of anger on Solomon's behalf. Then he went to those fish, took something from them, split open the belly of a fish, and there was the ring. Al-Hasan said: It was related to me that no one among the people sheltered him, and he went forty nights without food, and he would take refuge with a poor woman. One day, as he was on the bank of a river, he found a fish, brought it to the woman, and she split it open, and there was the ring. Al-Dahhak said: he bought a fish from a woman, split open its belly, and found his ring.

Regarding the period during which the kingdom was taken from him, there are two opinions. One: forty nights, as we mentioned from al-Hasan. The second: fifty nights, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The commentators said: when he put the ring on his hand, God restored to him his splendour and his kingdom, the birds shaded him, and he proceeded, and no jinn, bird, stone or tree met him without prostrating to him, until he reached his dwelling. Al-Suddi said: then he sent for the Satan, and he was brought, and he ordered that he be placed in an iron chest, then it was closed and locked over him, and he sealed it with his ring, then he ordered that it be thrown into the sea, and he remains in it until the Hour arises. Wahb said: he split a rock, put him into it, then bound it with iron and lead, then cast him into the sea.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatḥah (هَبْ لِي). On this there are two opinions.
One: "no one shall have it after me," said by Muqatil and Abu 'Ubaydah. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, in the two Sahihs, related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A 'Ifrit of the jinn escaped at me last night to cut off my prayer, but God empowered me over him, and I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that you might all look at him, but then I remembered the supplication of my brother Solomon: (My Lord, grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me), so I sent him back in humiliation."
The second: "it should not befit anyone to take it from me during my life, as the Satan did, who sat upon his throne," said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. He only sought this kingdom so that he might know that he had been forgiven, and recognise his station by the answering of his supplication, said by al-Dahhak. And in his kingdom at the time he made this supplication there was not the wind nor the devils ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾. Abu al-Jawza', Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿gently﴾ (rukhā'an). On this there are three opinions.
One: obedient, related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The second: that it is good, said by Mujahid. The third: soft, derived from softness (al-rakhāwah), said by the philologists.

If it is said: how did He describe it thus, after describing it in Surah al-Anbiya' [81] as violent? The answer: the commentators said: he would command the violent wind at times and command the gentle wind at other times. Ibn Qutaybah said: it was as though it would blow strongly when he willed, and become gentle when he willed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿wherever he directed﴾ (haythu aṣāba), meaning: wherever he intended and desired. Al-Asma'i said: the Arabs say, "So-and-so hit upon the right thing but missed the answer," meaning he intended the right thing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the devils﴾, meaning: We subjected the devils to him, ﴿every builder﴾ who builds for him whatever he wills, ﴿and diver﴾ who dives for him in the seas and extracts pearls, ﴿and others﴾, meaning: We subjected others to him, who were the rebellious devils, whom he subjected to himself until he bound them together in fetters because of their disbelief. Muqatil said: he bound them in iron. We have explained the meaning of ﴿bound together in fetters﴾ in Surah Ibrahim [49].

﴿This is Our gift﴾. The meaning: We said to him, "This is Our gift." On what is referred to there are two opinions.
One: it is all that was given to him, ﴿so bestow or withhold﴾, meaning: give to whom you will of the wealth, and withhold from whom you will. Bestowing (al-mann) is kindness to one who does not seek its reward.
The second: it refers to the devils subjected to him; the meaning is: bestow freedom upon whom you will, and withhold whom you will of them. The meaning of both opinions has been related from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without reckoning﴾. Al-Hasan said: there will be no consequence for you in this world or in the Hereafter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: there will be no reckoning for you on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: there is inversion in the speech, its implied sense being: "This is Our gift without reckoning, so bestow or withhold."

What follows this has already been explained [Saba': 37; al-Ra'd: 29; al-Anbiya': 83] up to His saying: ﴿the Satan has touched me﴾, because the Satan was given power over him, so he attributed to it what had befallen him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with affliction﴾ (bi-nuṣb). Most read with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn al-Sumayfa', al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read with fatḥah on both. Is there a difference between them? On this there are two opinions.
One: they are the same. Al-Farra' said: they are like al-rushd and al-rashd, al-'adam and al-'udm, al-hazan and al-huzn; Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said likewise. The commentators said: what is meant by nuṣb is the harm that befell him.
The second: nuṣb with a sukūn on the ṣād means evil, and with a vowel on it means exhaustion, said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

'Ā'ishah, Mujahid, Abu 'Imran, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and Abu 'Imarah, from Hafs, read "bi-nuṣub" with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the ṣād. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Jawza', and Hubayrah, from Hafs, read "bi-naṣb" with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād.

On what is meant by the punishment (al-'adhāb) there are two opinions. One: that it is the affliction that struck his body. The second: that it took his wealth and his children.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ (irkuḍ), meaning: strike the earth ﴿with your foot﴾, and from it comes "the horse struck (rakaḍat al-faras)." So he struck, and a spring of water gushed forth, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-mughtasal is the water, and it is also al-ghasūl. Al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth [from which he bathed, then walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth] and he drank from it. The majority of scholars hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him: he bathed in one and drank from the other.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigth)﴾. He had sworn that if God healed him, he would flog his wife one hundred lashes. On the cause of this oath there are three opinions.
One: that Iblis sat on the path of Job's wife in the guise of a physician, and she said to him, "O servant of God, there is a afflicted person here; would you treat him?" He said, "Yes, if he wishes I will cure him, on condition that when he recovers he says: 'You cured me.'" She came and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. By God, if He cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." Related by Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: that Iblis met her and said, "I am the one who did to Job what is upon him, and I am the god of the earth, and whatever I took from him is in my hand. Come, let me show you." He walked with her a short distance, then bewitched her sight, and showed her a deep valley in which were her family, her children and her wealth. She went to Job and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. Woe to you, how did he hear your words? By God, if God, Mighty and Majestic, heals me, I will flog you a hundred times." Said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.
The third: that Iblis came to his wife with a young goat and said, "Let him slaughter this for me now that he has recovered"; she informed him, and he swore to flog her. We have mentioned this opinion in Surah al-Anbiya' [83] from al-Hasan.

As for the bundle (al-ḍigth): al-Farra' said: it is whatever you gather of something like a fresh bundle; he said: whatever stands upon a stalk and grows tall, then you gather it, is a ḍigth. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is a bundle of twigs and reeds. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a bundle of grass, basil and the like. The commentators said: God rewarded his wife for her good patience by making it easy for him concerning her beating: he gathered for her one hundred stalks; it was said: one hundred ears of grain; it was said: they were palm fibres; it was said: they were of izkhir; it was said: they were sprigs of millet. He struck her with them in a single blow and did not break his oath. Is this specific to him, or not? On this there are two opinions.
One: that it is general, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn Abi Layla. The second: that it is specific to Job, said by Mujahid.

Section
The jurists have differed concerning one who swears to beat his slave ten lashes, then gathers them all and strikes him with them in a single blow. Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: he does not fulfil his oath, and our companions (the Hanbalis) also said so. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: if each one of them reaches him in the single blow, he has fulfilled his oath, and they argued from the generality of the story of Job, peace be upon him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾, meaning: in the face of the affliction with which We tested him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 38, verse 30–44 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿An excellent servant﴾ — He means Sulayman.

Regarding al-Awwab (the one who constantly turns back to Allah), there are views already mentioned in [Surat al-Isra': 25]. The most fitting of them in this context is that he is one who returns to Allah in repentance from the heedlessness and inattention that befall him.

Allah's words: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening,﴾ meaning after the decline of the sun, ﴿the swift steeds﴾, which are horses. There are two views regarding the meaning of al-safinat (standing on three legs).

The first: they are those standing on three legs, with the other foot resting on the tip of the hoof, whether of a forelimb or a hind limb. This is the view taken by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, and it was chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: "This is the most common stance of horses when they stop, as if they alternate between their legs." The poet said:

"The sufun (standing horses) have become accustomed, so that it is as if they stand on three, lamed."

The second: they are simply those standing, whether on three legs or not. Al-Farra' said: "On this view I have found the Arabs and their poetry indicating that it means standing only." Ibn Qutaybah said: "In the language of the Arabs, al-safin is the one standing still, of horses and others." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever desires that men stand for him in rows (sufunan), let him take his seat in the Fire." (p-128) That is, they continually stand for him.

As for al-jiyad, they are those swift in running. Regarding the reason for their being displayed before him, there are four views.

The first: he displayed them because he intended to fight an enemy of his. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: they were among the creatures of the sea. Al-Hasan said: "It has reached me that they were horses that came out of the sea, having wings." Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "They were twenty horses with wings." Ibn Zayd said: "The devils brought them out for him from the sea."

The third: he inherited them from his father Dawud, peace be upon him, and they were displayed before him. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih and Muqatil.

The fourth: he raided an army, defeated it and seized them as spoils, then called for them and they were displayed before him. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding their number, there are four views. The first: thirteen thousand, said by Wahb. The second: twenty thousand, said by Sa'id ibn Masruq. The third: one thousand horses, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The fourth: twenty horses, which we have already mentioned from Ibrahim al-Taymi.

(p-129) The exegetes said: They continued to be displayed before him until the sun set, so he missed the 'Asr prayer. He was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him about anything, so they did not remind him, and he himself forgot. When the sun set he remembered the prayer. ﴿So he said: "Indeed I have loved﴾ — the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatha — ﴿the love of good﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it is wealth, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. The second: it is love of horses, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. The two views return to one meaning, since by "good" he meant horses, and they are wealth. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call horses "al-khayr" (good). Al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ named Zayd al-Khayl "Zayd al-Khayr." The meaning of "I have loved" is: I preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord. Likewise, someone other than al-Zajjaj said: "'an" carries the meaning of "'ala" (on). Some of them said: The meaning may be: it distracted me from the remembrance of my Lord. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of [the expression] is: I loved a love, then he attributed the love to good. Ibn Qutaybah said: He called horses "good" because of the good that is in them. The exegetes hold that what is meant by "the remembrance of his Lord" is the 'Asr prayer; this was said by Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and others. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know whether the 'Asr prayer was obligatory or not, but his being occupied with the horses distracted him from a time in which he used to remember Allah, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾.

(p-130) The author says: The people of language say that it means the sun, though no mention of it has preceded. I do not think they have given this reflection its due, for in the verse there is an indication of the sun, namely His words "at evening." Its meaning is: they were displayed before him after the sun's decline, until the sun was hidden behind the veil. A pronoun cannot be used unless there has been a mention or an indication of a mention, in which case it stands in the place of a mention. As for al-hijab (the veil), it is that which conceals it from sight.

Allah's words: ﴿Bring them back to me﴾. The exegetes said: When the displaying of the horses preoccupied him from the prayer, so that he prayed it after its time had passed, he was grieved and angry, and said: "Bring them back to me," meaning: return the horses to me. ﴿So he began﴾ — Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, he set about — ﴿striking﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, he struck, striking.

As for al-suq, it is the plural of saq (shin/leg), like duur and daar. Ibn Kathir read al-su'q with a hamzah; Abu 'Ali said: other than the hamzah is better than it. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Muhaysin read "bi-al-suwuq," like al-ruus. Regarding what is meant by "striking" here, there are three views.

The first: that he struck them with the sword. Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding (p-131) His words, "so he began striking the shins and necks," that he said: "with the sword." Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: he struck their necks and shins with the sword. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he cut off their necks and shins. This is the view chosen by al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and the majority.

The second: that he began stroking the manes of the horses and their hocks out of love for them. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: he stroked them with his hand. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

(p-132) The third: that he branded their shins and necks and held them in the way of Allah, Most High. This is related by al-Tha'labi.

The exegetes hold the first view, though they have objected to the second, saying: What connection is there between their distracting him from the prayer and stroking their manes out of love for them? I do not know that the statement "out of love for them" is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas. They interpreted Mujahid's words "he stroked them with his hand" to mean: he undertook striking their necks.

If it is said: The first view is flawed, since the animal is not at fault; how then did he direct punishment at it and intend to satisfy his anger by killing it? This resembles the act of tyrants, not the act of prophets?

The answer: He would not have done so except that it had been permitted to him, and it is possible that something was permitted to him which is forbidden in our law. Moreover, if he slaughtered them they would have been an offering, and eating their flesh is lawful, so no negligence occurred. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When he struck their shins and necks, Allah Most High thanked him for that, so He subjected the wind to him in their place, which is finer in appearance, swifter in travel, and more wondrous in report.

Allah's words: ﴿And We did test Sulayman﴾, that is: We tried him and tested him by stripping him of his kingdom, ﴿and We cast upon his throne﴾, that is: upon his seat, ﴿a body﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was a devil. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Regarding the name of that devil there are three views. The first: Sakhr; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The scholars mentioned that he was a rebellious devil who had not been subjected to Sulayman. The second: Asif; this was said by Mujahid, except that he is not the believer who had the Greatest Name; however, some transmitters of the exegesis related that he is (p-133) Asif who had knowledge of the Book, and that when Sulayman was tested the ring fell from his hand and did not return; Asif said: "I will take your place until Allah accepts your repentance," and he stood in his place and conducted himself with fine conduct. This is not authentic, and no reliable transmitter mentioned it. The third: Haqbiq; this was said by al-Suddi, and the meaning is: we seated a devil upon his throne in his kingdom. ﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is: he returned. Regarding what he returned to, there are two views. The first: he repented of his sin; this was said by Qatadah. The second: he returned to his kingdom; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Sulayman's being tested in this way, there are five views. The first: he had a wife called Jarada, and between some of her relatives and a people there was a dispute; he judged between them with truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. He was punished because his inclination was not even toward both parties. Allah Most High revealed to him that a trial would befall him, and he did not know whether it would come to him from the heaven or from the earth. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: his wife Jarada was the dearest of the women to him, and she said to him one day: "My brother has a dispute with so-and-so, and I love that you judge in his favor." He said: "Yes," but did not do so, and he was tested because of what he had said. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: his wife Jarada had been taken by him as a captive in a raid, and she was a king's daughter who had embraced Islam, and she wept constantly by night and day in his presence. He asked her about her condition, and she said: "I remember my father and what I was in. If only you would command the devils to fashion his likeness in my house, so that I might console myself with it." [He did so], and whenever Sulayman went out, she and her maidservants prostrated to it for forty mornings. When Sulayman learned of this, he broke that image, punished the woman and her maidservants, then humbled himself before Allah Most High, seeking forgiveness for what had been in his house. So the devil was given power over his ring. [This is the saying of Wahb ibn Munabbih.] The fourth: he secluded himself from the people for three days, and Allah Most High revealed to him: "O Sulayman, you have secluded yourself from the people for three days and have not looked into the affairs of My servants, nor given justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer?" So the devil was given power over his ring. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. The fifth: he approached one of his wives during menstruation or otherwise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second view: that what is meant by the body cast upon his throne is that a son was born to him, and the devils gathered together, and some of them said to others: "If a son of his survives, it will not benefit you from the trial. (p-135) Our course is to kill his son or to cripple him." Sulayman learned of this, [so he commanded the clouds], which carried him away, and his son ran off into the clouds out of fear of the devils. Allah Most High rebuked him for his fear of the devils, and the child died, and he was cast upon his throne as a dead body. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The exegetes hold the first view. We will mention the story of his testing according to the view of the majority.

Indication of that:

The scholars differed about how the ring of Sulayman was lost, according to two views.

The first: he was sitting on the shore of the sea, and it fell from him into the sea. This was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: a devil took it, and regarding the manner of that there are four views.

The first: he entered the bathhouse one day and placed the ring beneath his bedding, and the devil came and took it and threw it into the sea, and the devil began saying: "I am the Prophet of Allah." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: Sulayman said to the devil: "How do you tempt people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will inform you." So he gave it to him, and he threw it into the sea, and Sulayman's kingdom departed, and the devil sat upon his throne. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: he entered the bathhouse, and placed his ring with his most trusted wife, (p-136) and the devil came to her in the form of Sulayman and took the ring from her. When Sulayman came out, he asked her for it, and she said: "I have already given it to you." Sulayman fled, and the devil came and sat upon his kingdom. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: he entered the bathhouse and gave his ring to the devil, and the devil threw it into the sea, so Sulayman's kingdom departed, and his likeness was cast upon the devil. This was said by Qatadah.

As for the story of the devil, most of the exegetes mention that when he took the ring he threw it into the sea, and his likeness was cast upon him, so he sat upon his throne and domineered over his realm.

And al-Suddi said: "He did not throw it into the sea until he fled from Solomon's place." Did [the wives of] Solomon get visited by him? On this there are two opinions. One: he was not able to have them, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: he would come to them during menstruation, and they rejected him, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib; the first is more correct. They said: he would issue unsound judgments and rule by what is not permissible, so the Children of Israel denounced him. Some of them said to others: "Either you have perished, or your kingdom has perished. Go to his wives and ask them." So they went, and the wives said: "By God, we have indeed rejected that." He remained in his state until the period of trial came to an end.

Regarding the manner of the Satan's distance from Solomon's place, there are four opinions.
One of them: Solomon found his ring and put it on, then came and seized the forelock of the Satan, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.
The second: when Solomon returned to his kingdom and the wind, the birds and the devils came to him, the Satan fled until he entered the sea, said by Mujahid.
The third: when forty days had passed, the Satan flew from his assembly, said by Wahb.
The fourth: when the Children of Israel denounced him, they came to him and surrounded him, then they unfolded the Torah and read, and he flew before them until he went to the sea, and the ring fell from him into the sea, and a fish swallowed it, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding how long the Satan remained, there are two opinions. One: forty days, said by most. The second: fourteen days, related by al-Tha'labi.

As for the story of Solomon, peace be upon him: when his ring was taken from him, his kingdom was lost, and he set off fleeing across the land. Mujahid said: he would ask for food and not be fed, so he would say, "If you knew me, you would give to me. I am Solomon," and they would drive him away, until a woman gave him a fish, and he found his ring in the belly of the fish. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Solomon set off until he reached the seashore, and he found fishermen who had caught a great deal of fish, some of which had begun to rot. He came to them asking for food. They said, "Go to those fish and take some from them." He said, "No, feed me from this." They refused him, so he said, "Feed me, for I am Solomon." A man among them leapt at him and struck him with a stick out of anger on Solomon's behalf. Then he went to those fish, took something from them, split open the belly of a fish, and there was the ring. Al-Hasan said: It was related to me that no one among the people sheltered him, and he went forty nights without food, and he would take refuge with a poor woman. One day, as he was on the bank of a river, he found a fish, brought it to the woman, and she split it open, and there was the ring. Al-Dahhak said: he bought a fish from a woman, split open its belly, and found his ring.

Regarding the period during which the kingdom was taken from him, there are two opinions. One: forty nights, as we mentioned from al-Hasan. The second: fifty nights, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The commentators said: when he put the ring on his hand, God restored to him his splendour and his kingdom, the birds shaded him, and he proceeded, and no jinn, bird, stone or tree met him without prostrating to him, until he reached his dwelling. Al-Suddi said: then he sent for the Satan, and he was brought, and he ordered that he be placed in an iron chest, then it was closed and locked over him, and he sealed it with his ring, then he ordered that it be thrown into the sea, and he remains in it until the Hour arises. Wahb said: he split a rock, put him into it, then bound it with iron and lead, then cast him into the sea.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatḥah (هَبْ لِي). On this there are two opinions.
One: "no one shall have it after me," said by Muqatil and Abu 'Ubaydah. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, in the two Sahihs, related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A 'Ifrit of the jinn escaped at me last night to cut off my prayer, but God empowered me over him, and I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that you might all look at him, but then I remembered the supplication of my brother Solomon: (My Lord, grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me), so I sent him back in humiliation."
The second: "it should not befit anyone to take it from me during my life, as the Satan did, who sat upon his throne," said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. He only sought this kingdom so that he might know that he had been forgiven, and recognise his station by the answering of his supplication, said by al-Dahhak. And in his kingdom at the time he made this supplication there was not the wind nor the devils ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾. Abu al-Jawza', Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿gently﴾ (rukhā'an). On this there are three opinions.
One: obedient, related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The second: that it is good, said by Mujahid. The third: soft, derived from softness (al-rakhāwah), said by the philologists.

If it is said: how did He describe it thus, after describing it in Surah al-Anbiya' [81] as violent? The answer: the commentators said: he would command the violent wind at times and command the gentle wind at other times. Ibn Qutaybah said: it was as though it would blow strongly when he willed, and become gentle when he willed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿wherever he directed﴾ (haythu aṣāba), meaning: wherever he intended and desired. Al-Asma'i said: the Arabs say, "So-and-so hit upon the right thing but missed the answer," meaning he intended the right thing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the devils﴾, meaning: We subjected the devils to him, ﴿every builder﴾ who builds for him whatever he wills, ﴿and diver﴾ who dives for him in the seas and extracts pearls, ﴿and others﴾, meaning: We subjected others to him, who were the rebellious devils, whom he subjected to himself until he bound them together in fetters because of their disbelief. Muqatil said: he bound them in iron. We have explained the meaning of ﴿bound together in fetters﴾ in Surah Ibrahim [49].

﴿This is Our gift﴾. The meaning: We said to him, "This is Our gift." On what is referred to there are two opinions.
One: it is all that was given to him, ﴿so bestow or withhold﴾, meaning: give to whom you will of the wealth, and withhold from whom you will. Bestowing (al-mann) is kindness to one who does not seek its reward.
The second: it refers to the devils subjected to him; the meaning is: bestow freedom upon whom you will, and withhold whom you will of them. The meaning of both opinions has been related from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without reckoning﴾. Al-Hasan said: there will be no consequence for you in this world or in the Hereafter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: there will be no reckoning for you on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: there is inversion in the speech, its implied sense being: "This is Our gift without reckoning, so bestow or withhold."

What follows this has already been explained [Saba': 37; al-Ra'd: 29; al-Anbiya': 83] up to His saying: ﴿the Satan has touched me﴾, because the Satan was given power over him, so he attributed to it what had befallen him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with affliction﴾ (bi-nuṣb). Most read with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn al-Sumayfa', al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read with fatḥah on both. Is there a difference between them? On this there are two opinions.
One: they are the same. Al-Farra' said: they are like al-rushd and al-rashd, al-'adam and al-'udm, al-hazan and al-huzn; Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said likewise. The commentators said: what is meant by nuṣb is the harm that befell him.
The second: nuṣb with a sukūn on the ṣād means evil, and with a vowel on it means exhaustion, said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

'Ā'ishah, Mujahid, Abu 'Imran, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and Abu 'Imarah, from Hafs, read "bi-nuṣub" with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the ṣād. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Jawza', and Hubayrah, from Hafs, read "bi-naṣb" with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād.

On what is meant by the punishment (al-'adhāb) there are two opinions. One: that it is the affliction that struck his body. The second: that it took his wealth and his children.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ (irkuḍ), meaning: strike the earth ﴿with your foot﴾, and from it comes "the horse struck (rakaḍat al-faras)." So he struck, and a spring of water gushed forth, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-mughtasal is the water, and it is also al-ghasūl. Al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth [from which he bathed, then walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth] and he drank from it. The majority of scholars hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him: he bathed in one and drank from the other.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigth)﴾. He had sworn that if God healed him, he would flog his wife one hundred lashes. On the cause of this oath there are three opinions.
One: that Iblis sat on the path of Job's wife in the guise of a physician, and she said to him, "O servant of God, there is a afflicted person here; would you treat him?" He said, "Yes, if he wishes I will cure him, on condition that when he recovers he says: 'You cured me.'" She came and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. By God, if He cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." Related by Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: that Iblis met her and said, "I am the one who did to Job what is upon him, and I am the god of the earth, and whatever I took from him is in my hand. Come, let me show you." He walked with her a short distance, then bewitched her sight, and showed her a deep valley in which were her family, her children and her wealth. She went to Job and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. Woe to you, how did he hear your words? By God, if God, Mighty and Majestic, heals me, I will flog you a hundred times." Said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.
The third: that Iblis came to his wife with a young goat and said, "Let him slaughter this for me now that he has recovered"; she informed him, and he swore to flog her. We have mentioned this opinion in Surah al-Anbiya' [83] from al-Hasan.

As for the bundle (al-ḍigth): al-Farra' said: it is whatever you gather of something like a fresh bundle; he said: whatever stands upon a stalk and grows tall, then you gather it, is a ḍigth. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is a bundle of twigs and reeds. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a bundle of grass, basil and the like. The commentators said: God rewarded his wife for her good patience by making it easy for him concerning her beating: he gathered for her one hundred stalks; it was said: one hundred ears of grain; it was said: they were palm fibres; it was said: they were of izkhir; it was said: they were sprigs of millet. He struck her with them in a single blow and did not break his oath. Is this specific to him, or not? On this there are two opinions.
One: that it is general, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn Abi Layla. The second: that it is specific to Job, said by Mujahid.

Section
The jurists have differed concerning one who swears to beat his slave ten lashes, then gathers them all and strikes him with them in a single blow. Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: he does not fulfil his oath, and our companions (the Hanbalis) also said so. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: if each one of them reaches him in the single blow, he has fulfilled his oath, and they argued from the generality of the story of Job, peace be upon him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾, meaning: in the face of the affliction with which We tested him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 38, verse 30–44 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿An excellent servant﴾ — He means Sulayman.

Regarding al-Awwab (the one who constantly turns back to Allah), there are views already mentioned in [Surat al-Isra': 25]. The most fitting of them in this context is that he is one who returns to Allah in repentance from the heedlessness and inattention that befall him.

Allah's words: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening,﴾ meaning after the decline of the sun, ﴿the swift steeds﴾, which are horses. There are two views regarding the meaning of al-safinat (standing on three legs).

The first: they are those standing on three legs, with the other foot resting on the tip of the hoof, whether of a forelimb or a hind limb. This is the view taken by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, and it was chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: "This is the most common stance of horses when they stop, as if they alternate between their legs." The poet said:

"The sufun (standing horses) have become accustomed, so that it is as if they stand on three, lamed."

The second: they are simply those standing, whether on three legs or not. Al-Farra' said: "On this view I have found the Arabs and their poetry indicating that it means standing only." Ibn Qutaybah said: "In the language of the Arabs, al-safin is the one standing still, of horses and others." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever desires that men stand for him in rows (sufunan), let him take his seat in the Fire." (p-128) That is, they continually stand for him.

As for al-jiyad, they are those swift in running. Regarding the reason for their being displayed before him, there are four views.

The first: he displayed them because he intended to fight an enemy of his. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: they were among the creatures of the sea. Al-Hasan said: "It has reached me that they were horses that came out of the sea, having wings." Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "They were twenty horses with wings." Ibn Zayd said: "The devils brought them out for him from the sea."

The third: he inherited them from his father Dawud, peace be upon him, and they were displayed before him. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih and Muqatil.

The fourth: he raided an army, defeated it and seized them as spoils, then called for them and they were displayed before him. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding their number, there are four views. The first: thirteen thousand, said by Wahb. The second: twenty thousand, said by Sa'id ibn Masruq. The third: one thousand horses, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The fourth: twenty horses, which we have already mentioned from Ibrahim al-Taymi.

(p-129) The exegetes said: They continued to be displayed before him until the sun set, so he missed the 'Asr prayer. He was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him about anything, so they did not remind him, and he himself forgot. When the sun set he remembered the prayer. ﴿So he said: "Indeed I have loved﴾ — the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatha — ﴿the love of good﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it is wealth, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. The second: it is love of horses, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. The two views return to one meaning, since by "good" he meant horses, and they are wealth. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call horses "al-khayr" (good). Al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ named Zayd al-Khayl "Zayd al-Khayr." The meaning of "I have loved" is: I preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord. Likewise, someone other than al-Zajjaj said: "'an" carries the meaning of "'ala" (on). Some of them said: The meaning may be: it distracted me from the remembrance of my Lord. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of [the expression] is: I loved a love, then he attributed the love to good. Ibn Qutaybah said: He called horses "good" because of the good that is in them. The exegetes hold that what is meant by "the remembrance of his Lord" is the 'Asr prayer; this was said by Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and others. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know whether the 'Asr prayer was obligatory or not, but his being occupied with the horses distracted him from a time in which he used to remember Allah, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾.

(p-130) The author says: The people of language say that it means the sun, though no mention of it has preceded. I do not think they have given this reflection its due, for in the verse there is an indication of the sun, namely His words "at evening." Its meaning is: they were displayed before him after the sun's decline, until the sun was hidden behind the veil. A pronoun cannot be used unless there has been a mention or an indication of a mention, in which case it stands in the place of a mention. As for al-hijab (the veil), it is that which conceals it from sight.

Allah's words: ﴿Bring them back to me﴾. The exegetes said: When the displaying of the horses preoccupied him from the prayer, so that he prayed it after its time had passed, he was grieved and angry, and said: "Bring them back to me," meaning: return the horses to me. ﴿So he began﴾ — Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, he set about — ﴿striking﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, he struck, striking.

As for al-suq, it is the plural of saq (shin/leg), like duur and daar. Ibn Kathir read al-su'q with a hamzah; Abu 'Ali said: other than the hamzah is better than it. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Muhaysin read "bi-al-suwuq," like al-ruus. Regarding what is meant by "striking" here, there are three views.

The first: that he struck them with the sword. Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding (p-131) His words, "so he began striking the shins and necks," that he said: "with the sword." Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: he struck their necks and shins with the sword. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he cut off their necks and shins. This is the view chosen by al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and the majority.

The second: that he began stroking the manes of the horses and their hocks out of love for them. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: he stroked them with his hand. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

(p-132) The third: that he branded their shins and necks and held them in the way of Allah, Most High. This is related by al-Tha'labi.

The exegetes hold the first view, though they have objected to the second, saying: What connection is there between their distracting him from the prayer and stroking their manes out of love for them? I do not know that the statement "out of love for them" is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas. They interpreted Mujahid's words "he stroked them with his hand" to mean: he undertook striking their necks.

If it is said: The first view is flawed, since the animal is not at fault; how then did he direct punishment at it and intend to satisfy his anger by killing it? This resembles the act of tyrants, not the act of prophets?

The answer: He would not have done so except that it had been permitted to him, and it is possible that something was permitted to him which is forbidden in our law. Moreover, if he slaughtered them they would have been an offering, and eating their flesh is lawful, so no negligence occurred. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When he struck their shins and necks, Allah Most High thanked him for that, so He subjected the wind to him in their place, which is finer in appearance, swifter in travel, and more wondrous in report.

Allah's words: ﴿And We did test Sulayman﴾, that is: We tried him and tested him by stripping him of his kingdom, ﴿and We cast upon his throne﴾, that is: upon his seat, ﴿a body﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was a devil. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Regarding the name of that devil there are three views. The first: Sakhr; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The scholars mentioned that he was a rebellious devil who had not been subjected to Sulayman. The second: Asif; this was said by Mujahid, except that he is not the believer who had the Greatest Name; however, some transmitters of the exegesis related that he is (p-133) Asif who had knowledge of the Book, and that when Sulayman was tested the ring fell from his hand and did not return; Asif said: "I will take your place until Allah accepts your repentance," and he stood in his place and conducted himself with fine conduct. This is not authentic, and no reliable transmitter mentioned it. The third: Haqbiq; this was said by al-Suddi, and the meaning is: we seated a devil upon his throne in his kingdom. ﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is: he returned. Regarding what he returned to, there are two views. The first: he repented of his sin; this was said by Qatadah. The second: he returned to his kingdom; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Sulayman's being tested in this way, there are five views. The first: he had a wife called Jarada, and between some of her relatives and a people there was a dispute; he judged between them with truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. He was punished because his inclination was not even toward both parties. Allah Most High revealed to him that a trial would befall him, and he did not know whether it would come to him from the heaven or from the earth. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: his wife Jarada was the dearest of the women to him, and she said to him one day: "My brother has a dispute with so-and-so, and I love that you judge in his favor." He said: "Yes," but did not do so, and he was tested because of what he had said. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: his wife Jarada had been taken by him as a captive in a raid, and she was a king's daughter who had embraced Islam, and she wept constantly by night and day in his presence. He asked her about her condition, and she said: "I remember my father and what I was in. If only you would command the devils to fashion his likeness in my house, so that I might console myself with it." [He did so], and whenever Sulayman went out, she and her maidservants prostrated to it for forty mornings. When Sulayman learned of this, he broke that image, punished the woman and her maidservants, then humbled himself before Allah Most High, seeking forgiveness for what had been in his house. So the devil was given power over his ring. [This is the saying of Wahb ibn Munabbih.] The fourth: he secluded himself from the people for three days, and Allah Most High revealed to him: "O Sulayman, you have secluded yourself from the people for three days and have not looked into the affairs of My servants, nor given justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer?" So the devil was given power over his ring. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. The fifth: he approached one of his wives during menstruation or otherwise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second view: that what is meant by the body cast upon his throne is that a son was born to him, and the devils gathered together, and some of them said to others: "If a son of his survives, it will not benefit you from the trial. (p-135) Our course is to kill his son or to cripple him." Sulayman learned of this, [so he commanded the clouds], which carried him away, and his son ran off into the clouds out of fear of the devils. Allah Most High rebuked him for his fear of the devils, and the child died, and he was cast upon his throne as a dead body. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The exegetes hold the first view. We will mention the story of his testing according to the view of the majority.

Indication of that:

The scholars differed about how the ring of Sulayman was lost, according to two views.

The first: he was sitting on the shore of the sea, and it fell from him into the sea. This was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: a devil took it, and regarding the manner of that there are four views.

The first: he entered the bathhouse one day and placed the ring beneath his bedding, and the devil came and took it and threw it into the sea, and the devil began saying: "I am the Prophet of Allah." This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The second: Sulayman said to the devil: "How do you tempt people?" He said: "Show me your ring and I will inform you." So he gave it to him, and he threw it into the sea, and Sulayman's kingdom departed, and the devil sat upon his throne. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: he entered the bathhouse, and placed his ring with his most trusted wife, (p-136) and the devil came to her in the form of Sulayman and took the ring from her. When Sulayman came out, he asked her for it, and she said: "I have already given it to you." Sulayman fled, and the devil came and sat upon his kingdom. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: he entered the bathhouse and gave his ring to the devil, and the devil threw it into the sea, so Sulayman's kingdom departed, and his likeness was cast upon the devil. This was said by Qatadah.

As for the story of the devil, most of the exegetes mention that when he took the ring he threw it into the sea, and his likeness was cast upon him, so he sat upon his throne and domineered over his realm.

And al-Suddi said: "He did not throw it into the sea until he fled from Solomon's place." Did [the wives of] Solomon get visited by him? On this there are two opinions. One: he was not able to have them, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: he would come to them during menstruation, and they rejected him, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib; the first is more correct. They said: he would issue unsound judgments and rule by what is not permissible, so the Children of Israel denounced him. Some of them said to others: "Either you have perished, or your kingdom has perished. Go to his wives and ask them." So they went, and the wives said: "By God, we have indeed rejected that." He remained in his state until the period of trial came to an end.

Regarding the manner of the Satan's distance from Solomon's place, there are four opinions.
One of them: Solomon found his ring and put it on, then came and seized the forelock of the Satan, said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.
The second: when Solomon returned to his kingdom and the wind, the birds and the devils came to him, the Satan fled until he entered the sea, said by Mujahid.
The third: when forty days had passed, the Satan flew from his assembly, said by Wahb.
The fourth: when the Children of Israel denounced him, they came to him and surrounded him, then they unfolded the Torah and read, and he flew before them until he went to the sea, and the ring fell from him into the sea, and a fish swallowed it, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding how long the Satan remained, there are two opinions. One: forty days, said by most. The second: fourteen days, related by al-Tha'labi.

As for the story of Solomon, peace be upon him: when his ring was taken from him, his kingdom was lost, and he set off fleeing across the land. Mujahid said: he would ask for food and not be fed, so he would say, "If you knew me, you would give to me. I am Solomon," and they would drive him away, until a woman gave him a fish, and he found his ring in the belly of the fish. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Solomon set off until he reached the seashore, and he found fishermen who had caught a great deal of fish, some of which had begun to rot. He came to them asking for food. They said, "Go to those fish and take some from them." He said, "No, feed me from this." They refused him, so he said, "Feed me, for I am Solomon." A man among them leapt at him and struck him with a stick out of anger on Solomon's behalf. Then he went to those fish, took something from them, split open the belly of a fish, and there was the ring. Al-Hasan said: It was related to me that no one among the people sheltered him, and he went forty nights without food, and he would take refuge with a poor woman. One day, as he was on the bank of a river, he found a fish, brought it to the woman, and she split it open, and there was the ring. Al-Dahhak said: he bought a fish from a woman, split open its belly, and found his ring.

Regarding the period during which the kingdom was taken from him, there are two opinions. One: forty nights, as we mentioned from al-Hasan. The second: fifty nights, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The commentators said: when he put the ring on his hand, God restored to him his splendour and his kingdom, the birds shaded him, and he proceeded, and no jinn, bird, stone or tree met him without prostrating to him, until he reached his dwelling. Al-Suddi said: then he sent for the Satan, and he was brought, and he ordered that he be placed in an iron chest, then it was closed and locked over him, and he sealed it with his ring, then he ordered that it be thrown into the sea, and he remains in it until the Hour arises. Wahb said: he split a rock, put him into it, then bound it with iron and lead, then cast him into the sea.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatḥah (هَبْ لِي). On this there are two opinions.
One: "no one shall have it after me," said by Muqatil and Abu 'Ubaydah. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, in the two Sahihs, related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A 'Ifrit of the jinn escaped at me last night to cut off my prayer, but God empowered me over him, and I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that you might all look at him, but then I remembered the supplication of my brother Solomon: (My Lord, grant me a kingdom that shall not befit anyone after me), so I sent him back in humiliation."
The second: "it should not befit anyone to take it from me during my life, as the Satan did, who sat upon his throne," said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. He only sought this kingdom so that he might know that he had been forgiven, and recognise his station by the answering of his supplication, said by al-Dahhak. And in his kingdom at the time he made this supplication there was not the wind nor the devils ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾. Abu al-Jawza', Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "al-riyāḥ" in the plural.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿gently﴾ (rukhā'an). On this there are three opinions.
One: obedient, related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. The second: that it is good, said by Mujahid. The third: soft, derived from softness (al-rakhāwah), said by the philologists.

If it is said: how did He describe it thus, after describing it in Surah al-Anbiya' [81] as violent? The answer: the commentators said: he would command the violent wind at times and command the gentle wind at other times. Ibn Qutaybah said: it was as though it would blow strongly when he willed, and become gentle when he willed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿wherever he directed﴾ (haythu aṣāba), meaning: wherever he intended and desired. Al-Asma'i said: the Arabs say, "So-and-so hit upon the right thing but missed the answer," meaning he intended the right thing.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the devils﴾, meaning: We subjected the devils to him, ﴿every builder﴾ who builds for him whatever he wills, ﴿and diver﴾ who dives for him in the seas and extracts pearls, ﴿and others﴾, meaning: We subjected others to him, who were the rebellious devils, whom he subjected to himself until he bound them together in fetters because of their disbelief. Muqatil said: he bound them in iron. We have explained the meaning of ﴿bound together in fetters﴾ in Surah Ibrahim [49].

﴿This is Our gift﴾. The meaning: We said to him, "This is Our gift." On what is referred to there are two opinions.
One: it is all that was given to him, ﴿so bestow or withhold﴾, meaning: give to whom you will of the wealth, and withhold from whom you will. Bestowing (al-mann) is kindness to one who does not seek its reward.
The second: it refers to the devils subjected to him; the meaning is: bestow freedom upon whom you will, and withhold whom you will of them. The meaning of both opinions has been related from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿without reckoning﴾. Al-Hasan said: there will be no consequence for you in this world or in the Hereafter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: there will be no reckoning for you on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: there is inversion in the speech, its implied sense being: "This is Our gift without reckoning, so bestow or withhold."

What follows this has already been explained [Saba': 37; al-Ra'd: 29; al-Anbiya': 83] up to His saying: ﴿the Satan has touched me﴾, because the Satan was given power over him, so he attributed to it what had befallen him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with affliction﴾ (bi-nuṣb). Most read with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād; al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn al-Sumayfa', al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read with fatḥah on both. Is there a difference between them? On this there are two opinions.
One: they are the same. Al-Farra' said: they are like al-rushd and al-rashd, al-'adam and al-'udm, al-hazan and al-huzn; Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said likewise. The commentators said: what is meant by nuṣb is the harm that befell him.
The second: nuṣb with a sukūn on the ṣād means evil, and with a vowel on it means exhaustion, said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

'Ā'ishah, Mujahid, Abu 'Imran, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and Abu 'Imarah, from Hafs, read "bi-nuṣub" with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the ṣād. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Jawza', and Hubayrah, from Hafs, read "bi-naṣb" with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād.

On what is meant by the punishment (al-'adhāb) there are two opinions. One: that it is the affliction that struck his body. The second: that it took his wealth and his children.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ (irkuḍ), meaning: strike the earth ﴿with your foot﴾, and from it comes "the horse struck (rakaḍat al-faras)." So he struck, and a spring of water gushed forth, and this is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-mughtasal is the water, and it is also al-ghasūl. Al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth [from which he bathed, then walked about forty cubits, then struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth] and he drank from it. The majority of scholars hold that he struck twice, and two springs gushed forth for him: he bathed in one and drank from the other.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍigth)﴾. He had sworn that if God healed him, he would flog his wife one hundred lashes. On the cause of this oath there are three opinions.
One: that Iblis sat on the path of Job's wife in the guise of a physician, and she said to him, "O servant of God, there is a afflicted person here; would you treat him?" He said, "Yes, if he wishes I will cure him, on condition that when he recovers he says: 'You cured me.'" She came and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. By God, if He cures me, I will flog you one hundred lashes." Related by Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn 'Abbas.
The second: that Iblis met her and said, "I am the one who did to Job what is upon him, and I am the god of the earth, and whatever I took from him is in my hand. Come, let me show you." He walked with her a short distance, then bewitched her sight, and showed her a deep valley in which were her family, her children and her wealth. She went to Job and informed him, and he said, "That is the Satan. Woe to you, how did he hear your words? By God, if God, Mighty and Majestic, heals me, I will flog you a hundred times." Said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.
The third: that Iblis came to his wife with a young goat and said, "Let him slaughter this for me now that he has recovered"; she informed him, and he swore to flog her. We have mentioned this opinion in Surah al-Anbiya' [83] from al-Hasan.

As for the bundle (al-ḍigth): al-Farra' said: it is whatever you gather of something like a fresh bundle; he said: whatever stands upon a stalk and grows tall, then you gather it, is a ḍigth. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is a bundle of twigs and reeds. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a bundle of grass, basil and the like. The commentators said: God rewarded his wife for her good patience by making it easy for him concerning her beating: he gathered for her one hundred stalks; it was said: one hundred ears of grain; it was said: they were palm fibres; it was said: they were of izkhir; it was said: they were sprigs of millet. He struck her with them in a single blow and did not break his oath. Is this specific to him, or not? On this there are two opinions.
One: that it is general, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ibn Abi Layla. The second: that it is specific to Job, said by Mujahid.

Section
The jurists have differed concerning one who swears to beat his slave ten lashes, then gathers them all and strikes him with them in a single blow. Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: he does not fulfil his oath, and our companions (the Hanbalis) also said so. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: if each one of them reaches him in the single blow, he has fulfilled his oath, and they argued from the generality of the story of Job, peace be upon him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾, meaning: in the face of the affliction with which We tested him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 38, verse 30–44 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿An excellent servant﴾ — He means Sulayman.

Regarding al-Awwab (the one who constantly turns back to Allah), there are views already mentioned in [Surat al-Isra': 25]. The most fitting of them in this context is that he is one who returns to Allah in repentance from the heedlessness and inattention that befall him.

Allah's words: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening,﴾ meaning after the decline of the sun, ﴿the swift steeds﴾, which are horses. There are two views regarding the meaning of al-safinat (standing on three legs).

The first: they are those standing on three legs, with the other foot resting on the tip of the hoof, whether of a forelimb or a hind limb. This is the view taken by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, and it was chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: "This is the most common stance of horses when they stop, as if they alternate between their legs." The poet said:

"The sufun (standing horses) have become accustomed, so that it is as if they stand on three, lamed."

The second: they are simply those standing, whether on three legs or not. Al-Farra' said: "On this view I have found the Arabs and their poetry indicating that it means standing only." Ibn Qutaybah said: "In the language of the Arabs, al-safin is the one standing still, of horses and others." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever desires that men stand for him in rows (sufunan), let him take his seat in the Fire." (p-128) That is, they continually stand for him.

As for al-jiyad, they are those swift in running. Regarding the reason for their being displayed before him, there are four views.

The first: he displayed them because he intended to fight an enemy of his. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: they were among the creatures of the sea. Al-Hasan said: "It has reached me that they were horses that came out of the sea, having wings." Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "They were twenty horses with wings." Ibn Zayd said: "The devils brought them out for him from the sea."

The third: he inherited them from his father Dawud, peace be upon him, and they were displayed before him. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih and Muqatil.

The fourth: he raided an army, defeated it and seized them as spoils, then called for them and they were displayed before him. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding their number, there are four views. The first: thirteen thousand, said by Wahb. The second: twenty thousand, said by Sa'id ibn Masruq. The third: one thousand horses, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The fourth: twenty horses, which we have already mentioned from Ibrahim al-Taymi.

(p-129) The exegetes said: They continued to be displayed before him until the sun set, so he missed the 'Asr prayer. He was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him about anything, so they did not remind him, and he himself forgot. When the sun set he remembered the prayer. ﴿So he said: "Indeed I have loved﴾ — the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the yā' with a fatha — ﴿the love of good﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it is wealth, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak. The second: it is love of horses, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. The two views return to one meaning, since by "good" he meant horses, and they are wealth. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call horses "al-khayr" (good). Al-Zajjaj said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ named Zayd al-Khayl "Zayd al-Khayr." The meaning of "I have loved" is: I preferred the love of good over the remembrance of my Lord. Likewise, someone other than al-Zajjaj said: "'an" carries the meaning of "'ala" (on). Some of them said: The meaning may be: it distracted me from the remembrance of my Lord. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The meaning of [the expression] is: I loved a love, then he attributed the love to good. Ibn Qutaybah said: He called horses "good" because of the good that is in them. The exegetes hold that what is meant by "the remembrance of his Lord" is the 'Asr prayer; this was said by Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and others. Al-Zajjaj said: I do not know whether the 'Asr prayer was obligatory or not, but his being occupied with the horses distracted him from a time in which he used to remember Allah, ﴿until they were hidden behind the veil﴾.

(p-130) The author says: The people of language say that it means the sun, though no mention of it has preceded. I do not think they have given this reflection its due, for in the verse there is an indication of the sun, namely His words "at evening." Its meaning is: they were displayed before him after the sun's decline, until the sun was hidden behind the veil. A pronoun cannot be used unless there has been a mention or an indication of a mention, in which case it stands in the place of a mention. As for al-hijab (the veil), it is that which conceals it from sight.

Allah's words: ﴿Bring them back to me﴾. The exegetes said: When the displaying of the horses preoccupied him from the prayer, so that he prayed it after its time had passed, he was grieved and angry, and said: "Bring them back to me," meaning: return the horses to me. ﴿So he began﴾ — Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, he set about — ﴿striking﴾. Al-Akhfash said: that is, he struck, striking.

As for al-suq, it is the plural of saq (shin/leg), like duur and daar. Ibn Kathir read al-su'q with a hamzah; Abu 'Ali said: other than the hamzah is better than it. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Ibn Muhaysin read "bi-al-suwuq," like al-ruus. Regarding what is meant by "striking" here, there are three views.

The first: that he struck them with the sword. Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding (p-131) His words, "so he began striking the shins and necks," that he said: "with the sword." Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: he struck their necks and shins with the sword. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: he cut off their necks and shins. This is the view chosen by al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farra', Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and the majority.

The second: that he began stroking the manes of the horses and their hocks out of love for them. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: he stroked them with his hand. This is the choice of Ibn Jarir and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

(p-132) The third: that he branded their shins and necks and held them in the way of Allah, Most High. This is related by al-Tha'labi.

The exegetes hold the first view, though they have objected to the second, saying: What connection is there between their distracting him from the prayer and stroking their manes out of love for them? I do not know that the statement "out of love for them" is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas. They interpreted Mujahid's words "he stroked them with his hand" to mean: he undertook striking their necks.

If it is said: The first view is flawed, since the animal is not at fault; how then did he direct punishment at it and intend to satisfy his anger by killing it? This resembles the act of tyrants, not the act of prophets?

The answer: He would not have done so except that it had been permitted to him, and it is possible that something was permitted to him which is forbidden in our law. Moreover, if he slaughtered them they would have been an offering, and eating their flesh is lawful, so no negligence occurred. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When he struck their shins and necks, Allah Most High thanked him for that, so He subjected the wind to him in their place, which is finer in appearance, swifter in travel, and more wondrous in report.

Allah's words: ﴿And We did test Sulayman﴾, that is: We tried him and tested him by stripping him of his kingdom, ﴿and We cast upon his throne﴾, that is: upon his seat, ﴿a body﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

The first: it was a devil. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Regarding the name of that devil there are three views. The first: Sakhr; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The scholars mentioned that he was a rebellious devil who had not been subjected to Sulayman. The second: Asif; this was said by Mujahid, except that he is not the believer who had the Greatest Name; however, some transmitters of the exegesis related that he is (p-133) Asif who had knowledge of the Book, and that when Sulayman was tested the ring fell from his hand and did not return; Asif said: "I will take your place until Allah accepts your repentance," and he stood in his place and conducted himself with fine conduct. This is not authentic, and no reliable transmitter mentioned it. The third: Haqbiq; this was said by al-Suddi, and the meaning is: we seated a devil upon his throne in his kingdom. ﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is: he returned. Regarding what he returned to, there are two views. The first: he repented of his sin; this was said by Qatadah. The second: he returned to his kingdom; this was said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding the cause of Sulayman's being tested in this way, there are five views. The first: he had a wife called Jarada, and between some of her relatives and a people there was a dispute; he judged between them with truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. He was punished because his inclination was not even toward both parties. Allah Most High revealed to him that a trial would befall him, and he did not know whether it would come to him from the heaven or from the earth. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: his wife Jarada was the dearest of the women to him, and she said to him one day: "My brother has a dispute with so-and-so, and I love that you judge in his favor." He said: "Yes," but did not do so, and he was tested because of what he had said. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: his wife Jarada had been taken by him as a captive in a raid, and she was a king's daughter who had embraced Islam, and she wept constantly by night and day in his presence. He asked her about her condition, and she said: "I remember my father and what I was in. If only you would command the devils to fashion his likeness in my house, so that I might console myself with it." [He did so], and whenever Sulayman went out, she and her maidservants prostrated to it for forty mornings. When Sulayman learned of this, he broke that image, punished the woman and her maidservants, then humbled himself before Allah Most High, seeking forgiveness for what had been in his house. So the devil was given power over his ring. [This is the saying of Wahb ibn Munabbih.] The fourth: he secluded himself from the people for three days, and Allah Most High revealed to him: "O Sulayman, you have secluded yourself from the people for three days and have not looked into the affairs of My servants, nor given justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer?" So the devil was given power over his ring. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. The fifth: he approached one of his wives during menstruation or otherwise. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second view: that what is meant by the body cast upon his throne is that a son was born to him, and the devils gathered together, and some of them said to others: "If a son of his survives, it will not benefit you from the trial. (p-135) Our course is to kill his son or to cripple him." Sulayman learned of this, [so he commanded the clouds], which carried him away, and his son ran off into the clouds out of fear of the devils. Allah Most High rebuked him for his fear of the devils, and the child died, and he was cast upon his throne as a dead body. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The exegetes hold the first view. We will mention the story of his testing according to the view of the majority.

Indication of that:

The scholars differed about how the ring of Sulayman was lost, according to two views.

The first: he was sitting on the shore of the sea, and it fell from him into the sea. This was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: a devil took it, and regarding the manner of that there are four views.
